key_terms.meaning: Bending where the moment acts about a principal axis of the section, so the neutral axis stays perpendicular to it and σ = M y / I applies directly.
An axis of the cross-section about which the product second moment I_xy is zero.
σ = M y / I, with σ the direct stress (N/mm²), M the bending moment (N·mm), y the distance from the neutral axis (mm) and I the second moment of area about that axis (mm⁴).
1/R = M / (E I), with R the radius of curvature (mm), E the Young's modulus (N/mm²) and I the second moment of area (mm⁴).
The product E I, the resistance of the beam to bending; doubling E I halves the curvature for the same moment.
Curvature of the cross-section in the direction opposite to the longitudinal curvature, produced by Poisson contraction (Poisson's ratio ν).
I_xy = ∫ x y dA over the section, in mm⁴; it measures how far the area is spread into the diagonal quadrants.
Bending where the moment is not about a principal axis, so I_xy ≠ 0 and the neutral axis is tilted away from the moment vector.
The line in the cross-section where the bending direct stress is zero; it passes through the centroid.
σ = [(M_x I_yy − M_y I_xy) x + (M_y I_xx − M_x I_xy) y] / (I_xx I_yy − I_xy²), linear in both x and y.
tan α = y/x on the neutral axis = −(M_x I_yy − M_y I_xy) / (M_y I_xx − M_x I_xy); α is measured from the x-axis.
I_u and I_v, the extreme values of second moment of area, found from I_xx, I_yy and I_xy by a Mohr-circle style construction.
u and v (mm), the deflections along the two principal axes, each obtained from its own curvature M/(E I).
δ = √(u² + v²) (mm), directed perpendicular to the neutral axis, not along the applied load.
Replacing a wall by a line of concentrated boom area A_i plus a wall term, valid because direct stress is nearly uniform across the small thickness.
A_i = (σ_actual / σ_boom) × (actual area), the equivalent lumped area used in the boom idealisation; for direct stress only it is the actual area.
A longitudinal stiffener in a wing or fuselage that carries direct bending stress and is treated as a boom.
A load whose line of action does not pass through the centroid or is not parallel to a principal axis, producing M_x and M_y together.
A through-depth change of temperature ΔT(y) that creates a free thermal curvature α ΔT / h, with α the coefficient of thermal expansion (per °C).
The stress left when expansion or curvature is prevented; only the part of the thermal strain that is restrained produces stress.

takeaways: When the moment acts about a principal axis, σ = M y / I and 1/R = M / (E I) are exact for the ideal beam, and the section also curves sideways by Poisson's effect, giving anticlastic bending.
A non-zero I_xy tilts the neutral axis away from the moment vector, and the stress becomes a linear function of both x and y.
The safest route for an unsymmetrical section is to find the principal axes, apply σ = M y / I about each of them, and add the results.
Deflection is built from two components along the principal axes, and the beam moves perpendicular to the neutral axis, so it does not travel along a skew load.
In a thin wall the direct stress is almost constant across the thickness, so the section reduces to booms carrying area plus thin shear-carrying walls.
A wing box with stringers is just an unsymmetrical-bending problem solved boom by boom.
A temperature gradient is a built-in curvature; a free beam bends with no stress, and only restraint converts that curvature into stress.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to derive the general unsymmetrical bending stress expression from the principal-axis form, locate the neutral axis, and then apply it to a thin-walled or stringer-stiffened section with a skew load, including the deflection.

bank.q: Derive σ = M y / I for symmetrical bending, stating every assumption behind it.
outline: Plane sections stay plane and rotate about the neutral axis
Linear strain variation with y, so linear stress by Hooke's law
Equilibrium of the normal force gives the neutral axis through the centroid
Moment equilibrium gives M = E I / R, hence σ = M y / I
Limits: elastic, small deflection, no shear lag, no local buckling

bank.q: What is anticlastic bending? Explain its origin and state how its curvature relates to the longitudinal curvature.
outline: Longitudinal extension causes lateral contraction by Poisson's ratio ν
Top surface contracts sideways, bottom surface expands
Cross-section therefore curves in the opposite sense
Transverse curvature ≈ ν / R for an isotropic material
Anti-elastic shape is why a flat plate bends into a saddle

bank.q: Explain why the neutral axis of a section with I_xy ≠ 0 is not perpendicular to the applied moment vector.
outline: Stress is a linear function of x and y when I_xy is present
Setting σ = 0 gives a straight line through the centroid
Its slope depends on I_xx, I_yy and I_xy, not on symmetry alone
Contrast with the principal-axis case, where the neutral axis is perpendicular to M
Physical picture: the stiffer direction pulls the axis round

bank.q: A section has I_xx = 12 × 10⁶ mm⁴, I_yy = 4 × 10⁶ mm⁴ and I_xy = 2.5 × 10⁶ mm⁴. It carries M_x = 8 kN·m and M_y = 0. Find the stress at the point (x, y) = (40 mm, 60 mm) and the angle of the neutral axis.
outline: Evaluate the denominator I_xx I_yy − I_xy²
Substitute into the general stress formula with M_y = 0
Keep units consistent: N and mm
Set σ = 0 and solve for y/x to get tan α
Check the sign convention for M_x and y

bank.q: For a cantilever of unsymmetrical section under a tip load, derive the deflection components along the principal axes and hence the magnitude and direction of the total tip deflection.
outline: Resolve the load into components on the principal axes u and v
Each component gives its own bending moment distribution
Integrate curvature M/(E I) twice with the correct boundary conditions
Combine u and v as vectors
Show the resultant is normal to the neutral axis

bank.q: A thin-walled channel section has flanges of area A_f and a web of thickness t. Idealise it into booms and calculate I_xx and I_yy.
outline: Direct stress is nearly uniform across the thin wall
Place boom area at each flange centroid
Add the wall's own second moment t h³/12 where needed
Use Σ A_i y_i² about the centroidal axis
Note when the wall term can be neglected

bank.q: A wing box idealised into four booms of areas A₁ to A₄ carries a vertical shear force through a point offset from the centroid. Determine the direct stress in each boom.
outline: Replace the offset load by a shear force at the centroid plus a torque
Bending moments M_x and M_y follow from the shear distributions
I_xx, I_yy, I_xy from the boom areas
Apply the general formula boom by boom
State that the torque is carried as shear flow, not direct stress

bank.q: A beam of depth h has a linear temperature difference of ΔT between its top and bottom faces and is free to bend. Find the free curvature and the stress if both ends are then fully restrained.
outline: Free thermal strain ε_T = α ΔT at each fibre
Compatible curvature gives 1/R = α ΔT / h
No stress when the beam is free
Full restraint applies an equal and opposite moment
Resulting stress varies linearly through the depth

bank.q: Compare the neutral-axis method, the k method and the principal-axis method for unsymmetrical bending, and say when each is most convenient.
outline: All three express the same linear stress field
Principal-axis method: rotate to axes where I_xy = 0, then use σ = M y / I twice
Neutral-axis method: work directly with the tilted neutral axis and the distance from it
k method: express stress through section constants k₁, k₂
Choice depends on whether principal properties or direct geometry are known
Numerical equivalence shown by one worked case

bank.q: Explain why an unsymmetrically loaded beam deflects perpendicular to its neutral axis rather than along the load direction.
outline: Curvature about each principal axis is driven by the moment about that axis
A skew load produces moments on both principal axes
The two curvatures add as perpendicular vectors
The resultant curvature vector is normal to the neutral axis
Consequence: a coupling between bending directions, absent in symmetrical bending
Practical effect on tip deflection of a swept wing

bank.q: Discuss the validity of the simple bending theory when applied to thin-walled aircraft sections, and state the corrections needed in practice.
outline: Assumptions: plane sections, elastic material, small deflections, no shear lag
Thin walls: direct stress nearly uniform across thickness justifies booms
Shear lag in wide skins makes stress non-linear across the width
Local buckling and crippling reduce effective boom area
Open sections twist under transverse load unless restrained
Closed boxes carry torsion by shear flow, needing shear centre treatment
Conclusion: use the theory for preliminary sizing, refine for certification

bank.q: A beam is subjected to both a bending moment and a through-depth temperature gradient. Show how the total stress is obtained and when the thermal part can be ignored.
outline: Thermal strain α ΔT is stress-free if free to expand
Restraint strain is the difference between actual and free strain
Superpose mechanical stress M y / I and restrained thermal stress
Fully free bending: thermal stress zero
Fully restrained: stress E α ΔT pattern
Partial restraint needs compatibility with the end conditions

bank.q: For a wing idealised as a tapered box with stringers, outline how the bending moment distribution is found and how the boom areas are chosen to keep stress within limits.
outline: Loads from lift and inertia give shear force along the span
Integrate shear to get bending moment, apply boundary conditions at tip and root
Boom areas from geometry; check I_xx and I_yy at several stations
Stress at each station from the general formula
Compare with allowable stress including buckling
Iterate boom areas until the design is balanced

bank.q: Describe how the deflection shape of an unsymmetrical beam can be computed numerically, and what checks confirm the result.
outline: Discretise the span into stations
Compute M_x, M_y at each station
Divide by E I about each principal axis to get curvature
Integrate numerically with the end conditions built in
Check equilibrium, zero deflection at supports, expected order of magnitude
Plot the deflected shape in both planes

glossary.def: The internal moment at a section, in N·mm, equal to the sum of moments of all loads on one side of the cut.
Normal stress acting along the length of the beam, in N/mm², produced by bending or axial load.
I = ∫ y² dA about a chosen axis, in mm⁴, measuring how far the area lies from that axis.
I_xy = ∫ x y dA, in mm⁴, zero when the axes are principal axes of the section.
The pair of perpendicular centroidal axes for which I_xy = 0 and I takes its extreme values.
The point where the area of the section balances; the neutral axis always passes through it in pure bending.
The line of zero bending stress in a cross-section.
The reciprocal of the radius of curvature, in mm⁻¹, equal to M/(E I) for bending about a principal axis.
The product E I of a beam, in N·mm², governing its resistance to bending curvature.
Opposite-sense curvature of the cross-section caused by Poisson contraction during longitudinal bending.
The ratio ν of lateral contraction to longitudinal extension in an elastic material, about 0.3 for aluminium.
A section whose wall thickness is small compared with its overall width or depth, so stress is nearly uniform across the thickness.
A concentrated area at a point of the idealised section, standing for the direct-stress-carrying material of the wall or stringer.
A longitudinal stiffener that carries direct bending stress and stiffens the skin against buckling.
The outer thin sheet of a wing or fuselage that carries shear and some direct stress.
A transverse load not aligned with a principal axis, so it produces moments about both principal axes.
The displacement of a point on the beam axis from its unloaded position, in mm.
The reduction of direct stress in a wide skin away from the stiffeners, so plane sections do not stay exactly plane.
Shear force per unit length along a thin wall, in N/mm, used for the torsion and shear carried by the skin.
The fractional length change per degree Celsius, symbol α, about 23 × 10⁻⁶ per °C for aluminium.
Stress produced when free thermal expansion or curvature is prevented by restraint.
Any support or connection that stops a beam from expanding, contracting or curving freely.
The hypothesis that a flat cross-section remains flat and rotates rigidly during bending, giving linear strain with depth.
The closed torsion-box part of a wing between the front and rear spars, idealised as skin plus stringers for bending analysis.
